title: Wire-tailed Swallow — pair at Bandhavgarh
subtitle: Two wire-tailed swallows at Bandhavgarh tiger reserve, India — one mid-flight, the other perched on a thorn twig. Captured at ISO 2500 on the OM-1 Mark II at 500 mm (1002 mm equivalent), 1/3200s f/5.6 to freeze the flying bird. The motion-frozen feathers and the perched bird's eye give noise-reduction and sharpening tools two distinct handling problems on the same frame.
editor_note: I disagree with darwain on this one — I prefer the Topaz edit; the bird in flight is too soft with the DxO version.
exif_summary: OM-1MarkII with OM 150-400mm F4.5 TC at 500mm (1002mm equivalent), 1/3200s at f/5.6, ISO 2500

critique.text: This is the original RAW image serving as the baseline. It exhibits a significant amount of luminance and color noise in the smooth background, likely from a high ISO setting. Both subjects—the perched swallow and the swallow in flight—are relatively soft, lacking crisp feather detail, and the flying bird has expected motion blur on its wings. Overall, the edits significantly improved the image by rescuing detail and reducing noise. In ranking how well the edits worked: Image 3 (DxO) is the most successful, providing excellent, natural-looking sharpness and clean noise reduction. Image 1 (Topaz Photo) is a solid second, offering great noise reduction but looking slightly more synthetic. Image 4 (Topaz Sharpen AI) is the least successful due to heavy over-sharpening artifacts and poor background rendering.

images.title: DxO PureRAW 6
images.caption: DxO using DxO DeepPrime wD3 with Lens Sharpness Optimization increased to 200 (Hard)

critique.text: Processed with DxO DeepPrime XD3, this image strikes the best balance of the set. The noise reduction is highly effective, removing the heavy grain of the RAW file while maintaining a slightly more natural background texture than Image 1. The 'Hard' Lens Sharpness Optimization (set to 200) has done an outstanding job extracting fine details in the perched bird's feathers and the flying bird's face without introducing the severe synthetic artifacts seen in the Topaz edits. The transition from the sharply rendered body to the motion-blurred wings of the flying bird feels authentic. This is the strongest overall image.

images.title: Topaz Photo
images.caption: Topaz Photo with noise reduction and custom subject sharpening using motion blur

critique.text: This edit applies Topaz Photo's noise reduction and custom sharpening. Compared to the RAW, the background noise has been completely eradicated, resulting in a very smooth, buttery backdrop. The sharpness of both birds is vastly improved; the perched bird shows good feather detail, and the flying bird's head is brought into focus while retaining the natural motion blur on the wing tips. However, the aggressive processing leaves the feathers looking slightly 'plastic' or synthetic upon close inspection, a common trade-off with heavy AI noise reduction. It is a massive improvement over the RAW but feels slightly less organic than the DxO version.

images.title: Topaz Sharpen AI
images.caption: Topaz Sharpen AI which is a discontinued product was used on this one, with motion blur

critique.text: Using the discontinued Topaz Sharpen AI, this image suffers from severe over-processing. While it aggressively attempts to correct the softness and motion blur, it introduces heavy, crunchy sharpening artifacts across both birds, making the feathers look unnatural, jagged, and harsh. Furthermore, noticeable edge halos are visible around the flying bird. The noise reduction is also inferior to the other edits; instead of a smooth out-of-focus area, the background looks mottled and blotchy. Compared to the RAW, it achieves higher perceived sharpness but at an unacceptable cost to overall image quality.
